title: As his own soul (1 Samuel 18:1–4)
hookLine: Jonathan loves David as his own soul and gives him his robe

lines: THE KING'S SON, AND A RIVAL.
cards: The fight is over. David stands before King Saul, who asks a plain question: whose son are you? The son of your servant Jesse, from Bethlehem.

That's all David says, as far as the text tells us. But someone else is in the room: Jonathan, the king's son. A fighter himself, who once climbed a rocky pass with only his armor-bearer to face a Philistine camp.
Later, Saul will tell him outright that as long as David lives, Jonathan's own kingdom won't be secure. Jonathan has every reason to see a rival.
And when David has finished speaking, the text turns from the king and looks at his son.

teach.b: Chapter eighteen opens: the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, "and Jonathan loved him as his own soul."

The Hebrew word under soul is nefesh, and it's wider than the English: life, breath, the self that's alive in you. Jonathan loves David the way a person holds on to their own life. And the phrase comes twice.
Two verses later Jonathan makes a covenant with David, a binding promise, and the reason given is the same: he loved him as his own soul.

teach.h: THE ROBE, THE SWORD, THE BOW.
teach.b: Then he strips off his robe and gives it to David. Then his garments, his sword, his bow, his belt. Everything a prince and a soldier would wear, handed to a shepherd.
The text doesn't explain the gesture.

Some readers hear the heir quietly handing over what marks him as heir. Others hear a friend dressing his friend in the best he has. Either way, nothing comes back: David gives nothing in these verses.
Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers, teaches that love which depends on some thing ends when the thing is gone, and love which depends on nothing never ends.
Its example of the second kind is the love of David and Jonathan: a friendship that isn't about what the other person can do for you.

how: Jews read the friendship of David and Jonathan in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets, and the teaching in Pirkei Avot about love that depends on nothing is studied with it.

o: a promise sealed between two friends
soul: life, breath, the living self
the robe that marks a king's heir

games.q: as his own soul — tap the pairs.

s: David gives Jonathan a gift in return
in these verses nothing goes back the other way. Jonathan gives, and David receives.
the phrase as his own soul comes more than once
Jonathan loves David as his own soul, and makes a covenant with him for that same reason.
the text explains why Jonathan gave his robe
it doesn't. some readers hear an heir handing over his place; others hear a friend giving his best.

games.q: you're Jonathan, the king's son. a shepherd has just become the hero of the army. what do you do?
o: keep your distance: he's a rival.
give him your robe, your sword and your bow.
ask your father to send him home.
games.why: Jonathan strips off his robe and hands it over, with his garments, sword, bow and belt, and makes a covenant with David.

practice: Let one friend come to mind, someone whose life you'd hold close.
Look around your own life for something to hand them, not something you were throwing out, but a book you love, an hour, a thing you made, and picture putting it in their hands.
If part of you wants to hold it back, let that be there too; if you pray, you can hold the verse, he loved him as his own soul.

wordCard.voice: nefesh. The Hebrew word for soul or self, wide enough to hold how Jonathan loved David, giving him his robe and his sword. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: as his soul, from nefesh, life or self, in 1 Samuel 18:1 and 18:3.

carryVoice: Your line: love that doesn't end. The kind that depends on nothing. See you tomorrow.
